questions.q: Why is a .env.example file safe to commit to a repository, even though .env itself is not?
options: It lists only the names of expected environment variables with no real values filled in
It contains the real production secrets but encrypted
It is automatically deleted before every commit
.env.example is identical to .env but renamed
questions.explain: .env.example documents what a service expects -- variable names only -- which is safe to share; the real .env file with actual values is gitignored.

questions.q: Why shouldn't a real .env file be committed even to a private repository?
options: Because "private" is not the same guarantee as "never leaves this machine," and the repo could be cloned, leaked, or exposed later
Because private repositories automatically reject .env files
Because .env files cannot contain valid environment variables
It's actually fine to commit .env to a private repo with no risk
questions.explain: Private repository access can change, be cloned, or be exposed through other means -- committing real secrets anywhere in git history is a lasting risk.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat a leaked RPC API key differently from a leaked deployer private key?
options: An RPC key leak typically means rate-limit abuse or a surprise bill, while a deployer key leak means an attacker can deploy or upgrade contracts as you
They are treated identically in every respect, with no difference in severity
An RPC key leak is always more dangerous than a deployer key leak
Deployer private keys cannot actually be leaked since they aren't stored anywhere
questions.explain: The damage from a leaked secret depends on what it can do -- an API key causes billing/abuse issues, while a deployer key can let an attacker act as you on-chain.

questions.q: How does a CI platform's secret store keep a value like DEPLOYER_PRIVATE_KEY out of the workflow file and commit history?
options: The value is set once in the platform's settings and injected as an environment variable only at run time, referenced by name in the workflow
The value is written directly into the YAML workflow file and relies on the repo being private
CI platforms do not support secrets at all -- values must be hardcoded
The secret is emailed to the deployer manually before each run
questions.explain: This extends the GitHub Actions pattern from Chapter 2, Lesson 8: secrets are referenced by name and injected at run time, never appearing in the workflow file itself.

questions.q: What two habits does this lesson recommend to limit the damage of an eventual secret leak?
options: Rotating keys on a schedule and scoping each key to least privilege
Using the same key for every service, and never changing it once set
Printing all secrets to CI logs so they're easy to find and replace
Giving every key full administrative access so nothing ever breaks
questions.explain: Rotation limits how long a leaked key stays useful, and least privilege limits what that key can actually do even if it leaks.
